title_en: Li Guang v. Shougang Heavy Machinery Company — appeal of patent infringement dispute
keywords_en: civil; patent infringement dispute; second instance; higher people's court; Beijing; natural person; legal person; patent law; determination of scope of patent protection; determination of equivalence of technical features; prior art defense; dismissal of claims; utility model patent; flag fluttering device; comparison of technical solutions; patent right; heavy machinery company patent infringement dispute
full_text_en:
Li Guang v. Shougang Heavy Machinery Company — patent infringement dispute (appeal)

Appellant (Plaintiff at First Instance): Li Guang, male, 47 years old, assistant engineer at Qinhuangdao Yaohua Glass Factory No. 2, Hebei Province.

Agent ad litem: Hu Jinguo, lawyer at Qinhuangdao Tianping Law Firm.

Appellee (Defendant at First Instance): Beijing Shougang Corporation Heavy Machinery Company.

Legal Representative: Xie Yourun, Manager.

Agent ad litem: Liu Ruihua, lawyer at Beijing Huaxia Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Zhao Yi, legal counsel of Shougang Corporation Heavy Machinery Company.

Appellant Li Guang, dissatisfied with the civil judgment (1993) Zhong Jing Zhi Chu Zi No. 807 of the Beijing Intermediate People's Court regarding the patent infringement case filed against Appellee Shougang Corporation Heavy Machinery Company, appealed to the Beijing High People's Court.

After trial, the Beijing Intermediate People's Court rendered its judgment on November 14, 1994, holding that: Article 59, paragraph 1 of the Patent Law of the PRC provides: "The scope of protection of a patent for invention or utility model shall be determined by the content of its claims." This means that only when the technical solution implemented by the actor is substantially identical to the patented technical solution can it be determined that the actor's conduct falls within the scope of patent protection, and thereafter a finding of patent infringement is established. The technical solution described in the claims, specification, and drawings of Plaintiff Li Guang differs from the flag-flying device of Defendant Heavy Machinery Company (hereinafter referred to as the Company) in two respects: 1. The internal structure of the hollow flagpole is different; 2. The arrangement of exhaust holes on both sides of the pole body is different. The above two differences are substantively not equivalent. The Defendant's flag-flying device does not fall within the scope of Plaintiff's patent. The Plaintiff's claim that the Defendant infringed its patent lacks factual and legal basis. Accordingly, the judgment dismissed Plaintiff Li Guang's claims.

Appellant Li Guang appealed, arguing that the technical solution adopted by the Appellee's flag-flying device is completely identical to the Appellant's patented technical solution, and the court of first instance erred in finding that the two are substantively not equivalent. The reasons: In the Appellant's patented technical solution, the flagpole body has upper, middle, and lower air chambers, the purpose of which is to save air source. This is not qualitatively different from the hollow pole body in the Appellee's flag-flying device. The Appellee's flag-flying device is more backward than the Appellant's patented technical solution; it not only lacks substantive technical breakthroughs but also wastes air source. The Appellant's purpose in leaving exhaust holes on one side of the pole body is to blow the flag and make it flutter; there cannot be a second purpose. Regardless of how the exhaust holes are arranged, their essence is the same. However, when comparing the essential technical features of the two technical solutions, the court of first instance set aside the common points and forcibly identified differences, thereby finding that the two are substantively not equivalent, committing an error in the determination of important facts. The Appellee's flag-flying device has fully fallen within the scope of patent protection of the Appellant, infringing the Appellant's patent rights. The Appellant requests the court of second instance to amend the judgment according to law.

Appellee Company argued in defense that the technical solution adopted by the Appellee's flag-flying device does not fall within the scope of patent protection of Appellant Li Guang, and the two have substantive differences. First, the internal structure of the flagpole is different. The Appellant's patented technical solution consists of a lower air chamber, a middle air chamber, and an upper air chamber, while the Appellee's flag-flying device does not have this feature. Second, the air outlet device of the Appellee's pole body is different. The Appellant's patented technical solution has a number of flag-raising exhaust holes and flag-hanging exhaust holes on the side of the pole body where the flag is raised. The flagpole of the Appellee's flag-flying device used at the 7th National Games is clearly different, and the effects are also different. The flagpole at the 7th National Games not only has no flag-raising exhaust holes, but the flag-flying device has several rows of asymmetrical air nozzles installed at the blowing holes on both sides of the upper part of the main flagpole corresponding to the length and width of the small flagpole. The holes of each air nozzle are flat, the angles of the centerlines of the air nozzles are different, and the centerlines of the air nozzles intersect the flag surface at different points, so that the flag surface is evenly stressed. This ensures that the flag flutters without wind and improves air utilization to save energy. In addition, the air inlet of the fan is also provided with an air volume control valve. The Appellee requests the court of second instance to dismiss the Appellant's appeal and affirm the original judgment.

The Beijing High People's Court, upon trial, found the following facts:

On November 5, 1990, Appellant Li Guang filed an application with the China Patent Office for a utility model patent named "Flagpole." On August 21, 1991, the national patent authority granted Li Guang a utility model patent with patent number 90222928. The claims of the patent are: "A flagpole consisting of a pole body, pulleys, and a flag rope, characterized in that: the pole body is hollow; the hollow cavity is divided into a lower air chamber, a middle air chamber, and an upper air chamber; on the side of the pole body where the flag is raised, a number of flag-raising exhaust holes and flag-hanging exhaust holes are provided; the lower part of the pole body is equipped with air inlet pipes respectively leading to the three air chambers and connected to an air source." In May 1993, commissioned by the Large Event Activities Department of the Preparatory Committee for the 7th National Games, Shougang Corporation accepted the task of developing flag-flying devices for the national flag and the Games flag at the main venue of the National Games, and instructed the Appellee Company to organize the completion, with the necessary funding borne by the Company. Thereafter, the Company began self-developing the flag-flying device and completed the design, manufacture, and installation of the flagpoles for the national flag and the Games flag at the main venue on schedule. The flag-flying device manufactured by the Company consists of a main flagpole, a flag, a small flagpole, fixed pulleys, a lifting rope, and a fan. The top of the main flagpole is decorated with a spherical flag crown ornament; the upper part of the hollow main flagpole is provided with flat blowing holes, and the lower part is provided with an air inlet hole; a fixed pulley is installed on the upper side of the main flagpole; at appropriate positions on the upper part of the main flagpole where the flag is raised, six rows of twelve asymmetrical flat-hole conical air nozzles are mounted at equal intervals and embedded in the blowing holes of the main flagpole; the air outlet of the fan is connected to the air inlet of the main flagpole through a flanged hose, and the air inlet of the fan is provided with an air volume control valve; the base of the main flagpole is fixed to the foundation, and the fan is fixed to the base. In July 1993, multiple news outlets reported on the process and features of the device developed by the Company's researchers and staff. Li Guang believed that the flag-flying device manufactured by the Company infringed his patent rights, and thus filed a lawsuit with the Beijing Intermediate People's Court on October 8, 1993. In addition, during the trial of this case, the Company submitted a utility model patent application specification for a "blow-type flagpole" (No. 85201537), which had expired on January 14, 1987. This patent application specification describes a flag-flying device for calm wind conditions, consisting of a flag, a hollow flagpole, a base, and a blower. When there is no wind or light wind, the blower is activated, causing air to rise along the hollow flagpole's conduit to the position where the flag is hung, and to be discharged from two vertical rows of small holes thereon, using a relatively strong airflow to blow the flag to flutter. Thus, at that time, the utility model patent for the blow-type flagpole had become prior art due to the termination of the patent.

The Beijing High People's Court held that: Appellant Li Guang's "flagpole" patented technical solution relates to a flag-flying device consisting of a hollow flagpole, pulleys, and a flag rope, which uses an air source to deliver wind through three air delivery pipes respectively to three air chambers inside the pole body, and by providing a number of exhaust holes on the side of the pole body where the flag is raised, to blow the flag to flutter. The "flagpole" manufactured by the Appellee Company also consists of a hollow flagpole, pulleys, and a flag rope; its working principle is to use an air source to deliver wind through one air delivery pipe into one air chamber inside the flagpole, and to blow the flag to flutter through an air outlet device provided on the side of the pole body where the flag is raised. The fundamental difference between the two is that Li Guang's patented technical solution has three air chambers inside the flagpole, while the Company's technical solution has only one air chamber inside the flagpole. Li Guang explicitly claimed protection only for a flagpole with three air chambers in his patent, whereas the specification of the "blow-type flagpole" utility model patent with a single air chamber had expired on January 14, 1987, and had become prior art before the filing date of Li Guang's patent. Therefore, the scope of protection of Li Guang's "flagpole" patent should not include single-chamber flag-flying devices. The Company's "flag-flying device" did not cover all the technical features of Li Guang's "flagpole" patent. Accordingly, Li Guang's grounds for appeal are untenable. The original judgment found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly. Therefore, in accordance with Article 153, paragraph 1, item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, the court rendered its judgment on March 24, 1995: dismiss the appeal of Appellant Li Guang and affirm the original judgment.

The litigation costs for the first instance and the second instance, each in the amount of RMB 2,010, shall be borne by Appellant Li Guang.
